newsitem.title: USA: CBOT considering new "world wheat" contract.
newsitem.headline: CBOT considering new "world wheat" contract.

text.p: Chicago Board of Trade officials are considering whether to add a so-called "world wheat" contract to the exchange and hope to make a specific proposal on a new wheat contract this year, the chairman of the CBOT said Thursday.

Speaking to reporters at the annual meeting of the National Grain and Feed Association, chairman Patrick Arbor said that adding a new wheat contract has been talked about for years by exchange officials, and that he hoped to move on the idea in 1997.

He said that currently the Chicago wheat contract -- which is for soft red winter wheat -- represents only a small portion of the wheat market, and that a new world wheat contract would more accurately reflect world wheat prices.
Arbor said the contract would not be designed to take business away from the Kansas City Board of Trade, where hard red winter wheat futures are traded.

On other issues, Arbor said he expected the CBOT membership to approve in April a new delivery system for corn and soybean futures contracts, despite some criticism that eastern producers will be at a disadvantage.
"We admit it may disenfranchise the eastern producers somewhat," said Arbor. But he said that it will benefit the bulk of producers. "We think the overall impacts will be positive," he said.

Addressing another controversial issue, Arbor said that the board has decided it would favor the lifting of a ban on agricultural trade options only if a requirement were made that the issuers of such options hedge an equal volume on the CBOT.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is studying whether to remove its ban on agricultural trade options. The National Grain and Feed Association and other farm groups strongly favor a lifting of the ban, saying it would provide another important risk management tool to the grains industry, and have not endorsed the CBOT's position for a hedging requirement.

Trade options are options on physical commodities entered into among commercial users of the commodity or its byproducts, and are offered outside the regulated futures markets. Agricultural commodities are the only physical commodities for which trade options are banned by the CFTC.

Arbor said the issue is a "competitive issue," and noted that trade options would be traded in an unregulated environment in contrast to the regulated futures market. He also maintained that it would be a good business practice to require an offsetting hedge and that it would reduce risks.
Arbor also said the board is considering expanding the hours of Project A -- the after hours electronic trading system for financial and agricultural products, and asked NGFA members for their input.
